draft.title: Stationary points and curve sketching
card: Stationary point
A stationary point is where f′(x) = 0. Solve this equation to find the x-values.
Nature
Check the sign of f′ on each side. Positive then negative is a local maximum. Negative then positive is a local minimum. The same sign on both sides is a stationary point of inflection.
Increasing
A function is strictly increasing where f′(x) > 0 and strictly decreasing where f′(x) < 0.
Example
For f(x) = x³ − 3x, f′(x) = 3x² − 3 = 0 gives x = −1 or x = 1. The function is decreasing for −1 < x < 1.
draft.remember: Set f′(x) = 0 to find stationary points, then use the sign of f′ to decide their nature.

a.q: What are the x-values of the stationary points of f(x) = x² − 6x + 5?
a.why: f′(x) = 2x − 6 = 0 gives x = 3. The values 1 and 5 are the x-intercepts, where f(x) = 0, not where f′(x) = 0.
a.clue: Differentiate first, then set the derivative to zero.

b.q: For f(x) = x³ − 12x, on which interval is f strictly decreasing?
b.why: f′(x) = 3x² − 12 = 3(x − 2)(x + 2). This is negative between −2 and 2, so f is strictly decreasing there. It is positive outside, where f is increasing, which is the tempting reversed answer.
b.clue: Factorise f′ and decide where it is negative.

problems.detail: The card says a function is strictly increasing 'where f′(x) > 0', which reads as the whole set where it increases. Under the VCE convention, a function can be strictly increasing at an isolated point where f′ = 0 (e.g. x³ at x = 0), and VCAA usually gives intervals with the endpoints included (e.g. [−1, 1] in the example). f′ > 0 is a sufficient condition, not the definition, so the card could mislead students on exam conventions.

check.summary: Both questions are correct and their explanations agree with the card. One minor issue: the card treats f′(x) > 0 as the definition of strictly increasing, which conflicts with the VCE convention of including endpoints where f′ = 0.

proposal.title: Stationary points and curve sketching
card: Stationary point
A stationary point is where f′(x) = 0. Solve this equation to find the x-values.
Nature
Check the sign of f′ on each side. Positive then negative is a local maximum. Negative then positive is a local minimum. The same sign on both sides is a stationary point of inflection.
Increasing

If f′(x) > 0 across an interval, except at isolated points where f′(x) = 0, f is strictly increasing there. So x³ is strictly increasing for all x, even though f′(0) = 0. With f′(x) < 0, f is strictly decreasing. Endpoints where f′ = 0 are usually included.
Example
For f(x) = x³ − 3x, f′(x) = 3x² − 3 = 0 gives x = −1 or x = 1. f′ < 0 between them, so f is strictly decreasing on [−1, 1], endpoints included.
proposal.remember: Set f′(x) = 0 to find stationary points, then use the sign of f′ to decide their nature.

a.q: What are the x-values of the stationary points of f(x) = x² − 6x + 5?
a.why: f′(x) = 2x − 6 = 0 gives x = 3. The values 1 and 5 are the x-intercepts, where f(x) = 0, not where f′(x) = 0.
a.clue: Differentiate first, then set the derivative to zero.

b.q: For f(x) = x³ − 12x, what is the largest interval on which f is strictly decreasing?
b.why: f′(x) = 3x² − 12 = 3(x − 2)(x + 2). This is negative between −2 and 2 and zero only at the endpoints, so f is strictly decreasing on [−2, 2]. Outside this interval f′ is positive, so the reversed answer is where f is increasing.
b.clue: Factorise f′ and decide where it is negative.

final.title: Stationary points and curve sketching
card: Stationary point
A stationary point is where \(f'(x) = 0\). Solve this equation to find the x-values.
Nature
Check the sign of \(f'\) on each side. Positive then negative is a local maximum. Negative then positive is a local minimum. The same sign on both sides is a stationary point of inflection.
Increasing

If \(f'(x) > 0\) across an interval, except at isolated points where \(f'(x) = 0\), \(f\) is strictly increasing there. So \(x^{3}\) is strictly increasing for all \(x\), even though \(f'(0) = 0\). With \(f'(x) < 0\), \(f\) is strictly decreasing. Endpoints where \(f' = 0\) are usually included.
Example
For \(f(x) = x^{3} - 3x\), \(f'(x) = 3x^{2} - 3 = 0\) gives \(x = -1\) or \(x = 1\). \(f' < 0\) between them, so \(f\) is strictly decreasing on \([-1, 1]\), endpoints included.
final.remember: Set \(f'(x) = 0\) to find stationary points, then use the sign of \(f'\) to decide their nature.

a.q: What are the x-values of the stationary points of \(f(x) = x^{2} - 6x + 5\)?
a.why: \(f'(x) = 2x - 6 = 0\) gives \(x = 3\). The values 1 and 5 are the x-intercepts, where \(f(x) = 0\), not where \(f'(x) = 0\).
a.clue: Differentiate first, then set the derivative to zero.

b.q: For \(f(x) = x^{3} - 12x\), what is the largest interval on which \(f\) is strictly decreasing?
b.why: \(f'(x) = 3x^{2} - 12 = 3(x - 2)(x + 2)\). This is negative between \(-2\) and 2 and zero only at the endpoints, so \(f\) is strictly decreasing on \([-2, 2]\). Outside this interval \(f'\) is positive, so the reversed answer is where \(f\) is increasing.
b.clue: Factorise \(f'\) and decide where it is negative.
